::: {.callout-tip title="How to read these notes"}
Each lecture is a standalone page written to be read straight through. The
recording stays one click away: the chapter links its video under the title,
and every section carries a timestamp that opens the lecture at the moment the
idea is introduced, so you can watch the derivation being built when the prose
is not enough. Sections, equations and figures are numbered and individually
linkable.
:::

## Lectures {#lectures}

The course runs to twenty lectures and one discussion section. Chapters are
published as they are written, in course order; the [roadmap](#roadmap) groups
them by theme.

## What these notes are

The [official CS229 notes](https://cs229.stanford.edu/) are the formal account
of the course, and a good one. What they cannot carry is the lecture itself:
the order in which Andrew Ng motivates an idea before he formalises it, the
picture he draws to make an update rule obvious, the question from the room
that exposes the step everyone was about to skip.

These notes are written from the Autumn 2018 recordings rather than from the
official notes, and they are meant to sit beside both. Each page aims to be:

- **Faithful to the lecture** — it follows what was taught and why, and links
  each section to the moment in the video where it happens.
- **Complete in its mathematics** — the derivations done at the board are
  written out in full, with every symbol defined.
- **A bridge, not a copy** — where the official notes go further, the chapter
  says which section to read next rather than reproducing it.

## Roadmap {#roadmap}

::: {.cs-roadmap}
1. **Supervised learning** — linear and logistic regression, generalized linear models, generative learning, support vector machines and kernels
2. **Generalization** — bias and variance, model selection, learning theory
3. **Trees and neural networks** — decision trees and ensembles, neural networks and backpropagation
4. **Applying machine learning** — debugging learning algorithms and error analysis
5. **Unsupervised learning** — k-means, EM, factor analysis, PCA and ICA
6. **Reinforcement learning** — MDPs, value and policy iteration, continuous states, LQR
:::

## Contributing

Found an error? Corrections are genuinely welcome — there is an **Edit this page**
link at the bottom of every lecture, which opens a pull request in your browser.
For anything larger, open an [issue](https://github.com/raimbekovm/cs229-2018-notes/issues).
